title: Semantic Content Production | Briefs to Published Pages
description: The execution service. Each node of the topical map becomes a brief, a written page, a configured page, and a published page in roadmap order.
h1: Semantic Content Production: Briefs, Writing, and Publishing in Sequence
standfirst: Semantic Content Production turns each node of the topical map into a published page. Each page gets a brief, the writing, the on-page configuration, and its internal links. The source term vector governs the wording, and the roadmap sets the publishing order.

sections.heading: What pipeline does Semantic Content Production run for each page?
sections.html:
What pipeline does Semantic Content Production run for each page?

Every page passes all six stages. The check at each stage is a written gate, not a feeling.

Brief

Input
The map node: entity, attributes, predicate, page decision.
Output
The brief document.
Check
Brief QA against the node and the vocabulary.

Draft

Input
The brief.
Output
The first draft, section by section.
Check
Vocabulary check: canonical terms only, head term as subject.

Edit

Input
The draft.
Output
The edited page.
Check
Sentence rules: one fact per sentence, no padding, no repeated phrases across pages.

Configure

Input
The edited page.
Output
The CMS page with title, ids, schema, captions, and internal links.
Check
Template QA: block order, main component, identity.

Publish

Input
The configured page.
Output
The live page, in roadmap order.
Check
Index check within the crawl cycle.

Measure

Input
The live page.
Output
Search Console per template, clicks and impressions by page group.
Check
90-day review: keep, rewrite, or merge.

sections.heading: How does Content Production work?
sections.html:
How does Content Production work?

Production is the map, executed in order.

No page is written without a brief. No brief is written without a node on the map. No page goes live out of sequence. The discipline separates a content network from a blog. The six-stage pipeline below runs for every node, and each stage carries a check the page passes or fails.

sections.heading: Which writing rules does Semantic Content Production apply to every page?
sections.html:
Which writing rules does Semantic Content Production apply to every page?

  1. Head term as subjectThe heaviest term in the query is the subject of the opening sentence and of the triples.
  2. One fact per sentenceA verifiable claim sits alone. Compound claims are split.
  3. Consensus facts in consensus wordingFacts the field agrees on use the field's terms. Unique claims carry their evidence in the same block.
  4. No paddingSentences that list uses without naming an attribute are cut. Length is not a target.
  5. No shared phrases across pagesAn n-gram check runs across the site before launch and every ninety days. Repeated four-word phrases are rewritten.
  6. Captions under every imageOne declarative sentence: entity, attribute, and relation to the section.

sections.heading: Which Google documents does Content Production build on?
sections.html:
Which Google documents does Content Production build on?

Patents describe systems Google has invented. They are not confirmed ranking factors. The work is built so a page passes the check each document describes.

  • US 9,940,367 B1: Scoring candidate answer passages (Google)A Google patent describes scoring answer passages by term match and position; the head term opens each block here.
  • US 11,354,342 B2: Contextual estimation of link information gain (Google)A Google patent describes scoring the information a document adds beyond pages already viewed; unique claims here carry their evidence.

sections.heading: Who is Semantic Content Production for?
sections.html:
Who is Semantic Content Production for?

Teams that want the map executed to the standard it was built to

The architecture exists. The team does not have the hours.

Sites publishing in more than one language

Same brief, same block sequence, native-language editors for German, Spanish, and Italian.

Sites whose current content failed the audit

Rewrite in sequence, page by page, against the new vocabulary.

Not the right fit

A site without a map or an audit. Production without page decisions produces the cannibalization it is meant to prevent.

sections.heading: Questions about Content Production
sections.html:
Questions about Content Production

Who writes the pages?The in-house editorial team under Abad Aslam, with native-language editors for German, Spanish, and Italian. Every page has a named editor who signs off the checks.
Can our writers use your briefs and your checks?Yes. The architecture path covers exactly that. The brief format, the vocabulary, and the six checks are handed over in the workshop.
How is the keep, rewrite, or merge call made at ninety days?The page decision is revisited first. A page that fails the page test on review is merged into its parent. One that passes is rewritten against the live results.
Which CMS platforms do you publish into?WordPress, Shopify, Wix, Squarespace, and Next.js with a headless CMS. The configure stage is done in your system, not in a document.
Do you write product descriptions and listings?Yes, as item sets. Each item gets sentences that are true only of that item. The n-gram check catches template filler across the set.
Does Content Production rewrite existing articles on their current URLs?Existing pages are matched to map nodes first. A page that matches a node is rewritten in sequence on its current URL. Pages with no node get a merge or prune decision.
How do we review pages before they go live?Your named contact reviews each edited page before the configure stage. Fact corrections go back into the draft. The named editor then signs off the checks again.
How are disagreements over wording handled?Facts go to your subject-matter contact. Vocabulary follows the source term vector, so a disputed term changes there and then site-wide. One-off wording that breaks the vocabulary is flagged before it ships.
Do you translate our English pages?No page is translated word for word. A native-language editor writes each language version from the same brief. Each version follows its own vocabulary.
What access does Content Production need?An editor-level CMS login for the configure and publish stages. Read access to Search Console for the measure stage. A subject-matter contact who answers fact questions.
